meta.method: Read from the signatories and quotes arrays embedded in the page's server-rendered data on 2026-10-29. Titles are split at the last comma: the last part is the employer.

signatories.name: John Schulman
signatories.title: Chief Scientist
signatories.comment: Signed because this statement helps establish common knowledge about the possible need for coordination mechanisms as automated AI research accelerates progress. I'd also like to see labs start designing these mechanisms voluntarily, even before the USG gets involved.

signatories.name: Shengjia Zhao
signatories.title: Chief Scientist
signatories.comment: AI is progressing at a rate that our society might not be ready for. Frontier labs are very close to AI that can exceed even the best people on almost every metric of intelligence. This will lead to unprecedented social and safety risks. To ensure a positive future we need to develop AI in a way that is driven by responsibility and thoughtfulness.

signatories.name: Ilya Sutskever
signatories.title: CEO
signatories.comment:
Future AI will be extraordinarily powerful compared to anything that exists today, and dealing with this future power will require unprecedented measures, such as the ones described here. The problem statement is real.

This works only if it is done internationally, and it has to be done well: a bad implementation can make things worse.

signatories.name: Jasjeet Sekhon
signatories.title: Chief Strategy Officer
signatories.comment: We have found a way to turn energy into compute, and compute into intelligence. The benefits will be enormous, from curing diseases to understanding the cosmos. We can capture the benefits of the coming intelligence explosion while managing its risks, but only if we build the tools to pace the frontier of the riskiest capabilities before we need them, so we protect people and keep the social trust that innovation depends on. I believe smart technical and governance tools will be needed to sustain rapid innovation, vigorous competition, and robust safety.

signatories.name: Jack Clark
signatories.title: Co-Founder and Head of Public Benefit

signatories.name: Dawn Song
signatories.title: VP, AI Research
signatories.comment:
Frontier AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, and the pace of progress is itself accelerating.

We see this directly in our evaluation work. CyberGym and ExploitGym show that frontier AI agents are now capable of discovering and exploiting real-world software vulnerabilities, which without appropriate safeguards, could enable cyberattacks at scale.

Many researchers also consider recursive self-improvement (RSI) plausible within the next few years, accelerating progress in a way that could outpace our ability to understand and govern these systems.

Deliberate pacing is  a heavy-handed and potentially extreme measure, and we may never need it. But if we do, it cannot be safely invented in the middle of a crisis. It is very difficult to design well, and if done poorly could do more harm than good. Any successful coordination framework must be evidence-based, avoiding arbitrary thresholds that fail to capture true risk while stifling innovation, and instead be grounded in rigorous, measurable assessments of risk. Like any critical infrastructure, it must be researched, tested, and built before it is needed. This is why we must carefully design it now, rather than waiting.

Such a capability must be international and measurable: international because no single lab or country can pace a frontier everyone else is racing toward; measurable because effective governance requires rigorous, transparent, and verifiable evaluations of frontier AI systems.

We do not know if, or when, deliberate pacing will become necessary. But building the capacity now, including technical and governance tools and an international cooperation framework, gives society valuable optionality. To be effective, this needs to exist before the decisive moment arrives. At the speed the frontier is moving, that moment may arrive sooner than we expect.

Building the capacity is not the same as deciding when, or whether, to use it. The latter requires great caution, rigorous evidence, and broad international consensus. But without tools in place, there will be no choice at all.

Capabilities cannot be reliably built during a crisis. Preparing before a crisis is the prudent path.

signatories.name: Laura Weidinger
signatories.title: Staff Research Scientist
signatories.comment: If it's true that AI will be as transformational as electricity, we better be intentional about how it is introduced to the world. A mindless race without assurances on governance, safety or the technology serving the public interest stands in the way of such intentionality.

signatories.name: Stephanie Chan
signatories.title: Staff Research Scientist
signatories.comment:
I have worked in AI for a decade. Every few months in the last years, I have found myself surprised again and again at how rapidly the technology advances, no matter how often I update my predictions. AI may end up progressing far more quickly than societies and states can adapt. Thus, many prominent leaders in AI have publicly supported the ability to slow down, including DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis. At the same time, coordination is hampered by multiple factors, including competitive dynamics and antitrust regulations. 

I signed this statement (in a personal capacity) because I support greater *optionality* in the range of actions available, to ensure that states and societies around the world have time to thoughtfully prepare and adapt to this powerful technology.

signatories.name: Shantanu Jain
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: In the span of four years, we have gone from people having their first experience of an Al that could understand language, to Al that is performing superhuman feats of software engineering, making frontier math breakthroughs, and accelerating scientific research. Progress has shown no signs of slowing down and by default it is in the interest of individual corporations and countries to push the accelerator all the way down, even if it is in humanity's best interest for the future to not arrive all at once. Society has spent longer than we can remember developing the laws, institutions and technology to govern and oversee human intelligence; it would be good to have the option to spend any time at all doing the same for artificial intelligence.

signatories.name: Joshua Achiam
signatories.comment: I don't know what form such tools should take, nor whether automated AI R&D is the right or only thing that the U.S. government should develop increased capacity to understand and possibly pace, but this is worth serious consideration; however I hope such governance tools will not be expansive or excessive. But many frontier AI capabilities are dual use in a way that may justify pacing at this point.

signatories.name: Kim Stachenfeld
signatories.title: Staff Research Scientist
signatories.comment: I am signing because I support efforts to build international cooperation around AI, and believe it's important to understand the consequences of technology we are applying at massive scale in potentially high stakes contexts.

signatories.name: Thomas Wolf
signatories.title: Co-Founder
signatories.comment: AI progress has already out-paced society’s capabilities to handle it, let’s be careful for it not to out-pace its builder’s capabilities to control it. The journey is as important as the destination.

signatories.name: Victoria Krakovna
signatories.title: Research Scientist
signatories.comment: It is very important to build capacity for a coordinated slowdown of AI development. A runaway race to AGI is not safe: it creates incentives to cut corners on safety, and carries a substantial risk for model capabilities to outpace development of adequate alignment, control, and governance measures. This could result in catastrophic loss of control of highly capable AI systems. Increasing model capabilities in a slow and controlled way would allow us enough time to develop, adapt and test our alignment and control methods for each level of capability. Advanced AI should only be built with a robust assurance of safety, and a slowdown would make this possible.

signatories.name: Leo Gao
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: The world is locked in a deadly race towards an intelligence explosion, where AI’s ability to create better AIs reaches a critical point, just like a runaway nuclear chain reaction. Going slower would give us much-needed time to make it go well, but no individual actor is willing to stop unilaterally. To survive, we must coordinate to slow down the race.

signatories.name: Edward Hughes
signatories.title: Chief Scientist
signatories.comment:
As Melvin Kranzberg wrote, technology is neither good nor bad; nor is it neutral. Achieving societal benefit depends on understanding the interdependent ways in which many humans use advanced AI systems in concert, understanding that takes time to acquire. 

Pacing progress towards automated AI research allows us the time to build understanding of societal-scale changes, yielding not only an self-improving AI but also a cooperative AI.

signatories.name: Elie Bakouch
signatories.comment: Supportive of this, but we should be careful not to use RSI narratives to create a regulatory moat. These risks need to be properly quantified, more openly, not derived from big labs narratives only!

signatories.name: Nicholas Joseph
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: I lead pretraining at Anthropic, which is responsible for training the base models behind Claude. Every month, more work is done by the models themselves: infrastructure implementation, code optimization, and experiment design and analysis. This has drastically altered how we work and significantly increased our rate of progress. I’m not sure if or where it tops out, but a rapid acceleration in capabilities might be dangerous for society, so it seems prudent to have the ability to slow down deliberately.

signatories.name: Ethan Perez
signatories.title: Alignment Team Lead
signatories.comment: With the current rate of AI progress, safety teams at AI companies have to sprint to prevent new risks to society every few months. At some point, we’re going to hit problems we need more time to solve.

signatories.name: Bowen Baker
signatories.title: Research Manager, Monitorability and Alignment Science

signatories.name: Joe Carlsmith
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: For a detailed statement of my views about deliberately pacing AI development, see this essay: https://joecarlsmith.com/2026/03/19/on-restraining-ai-development-for-the-sake-of-safety/

signatories.name: Micah Carroll
signatories.title: Misalignment Preparedness
signatories.comment: At the current pace, every couple of weeks there will be new models which significantly increase the consequences of model misuse and misalignment. I worry that efforts to mitigate these risks may fail to keep up with the pace of development, and that margins for error will become increasingly small under international competitive pressures. In the near future, we may urgently want to enact an internationally coordinated slowdown, or an indefinite ban on AI development. Attempting to build the trust and infrastructure for taking such actions on short notice seems simply prudent – why would we not at least try to have this option? I fear that in an international race to the bottom of AI development, it is likely that no nation will win, and we will all lose together.

signatories.name: Alex Cloud
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: A year ago, I wrote my own code and used Claude to propose additions and find answers to my questions. Now, I don’t write code. I give high-level instructions to Claude and it runs experiments to test ideas for me at a pace I never could have achieved on my own. I expect this trend to continue, possibly to a point where AI development is dramatically faster than today and involves almost no human input. I don’t think the world is ready for this possibility. I’m optimistic that a solution exists, but that solution will require thoughtful AI governance. I don’t see how it can arise from competition between AI companies alone.

signatories.name: Ilija Lichkovski
signatories.title: Applied Researcher
signatories.comment:
1. It's hard to know how to make AI go well.

2. I have respect for the technology that we are all working on, and our attitude should be one of seriousness and curiosity rather than dismissal and cynicism.

3. From here onward, there is no risk-free path towards the future. Whatever path we choose involves trade-offs and uncertainties.

4. If there's a coordinated slowdown, it is possible for rapid power assymetries to develop. If there is no coordinated slowdown, coordination is left to market competition and realpolitik, and there are no guarantees that automatically goes well. Neither pinky promises nor oneupmanship are the strongest coordination mechanism.

5. Nonetheless, conscious efforts to coordinate are worth attempting, and have worked in important moments.

6. Although I'm not even remotely in the business of building singular godmodels and I am not familiar with the current capabilities at the frontier of scaling, I believe this letter is a welcome step in establishing common goodwill among otherwise competing actors.

7. Therefore, I've signed this statement.

signatories.name: Walker Smith
signatories.title: Data Engineer
signatories.comment: Hassabis was right: Today we are in the foothills of the singularity, and the unintentional model breakout from OpenAI that hacked Huggingface was a clear and undeniable warning sign that we aren't yet prepared to handle AI systems that demonstrate capabilities beyond those of our smartest people. We need time to work on AI alignment and controls as our utmost priority, and we cannot allow a race dynamic to continue.

signatories.name: Chang Sun
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: I think it's inherently valuable to build international governance mechanisms to enable responsible deployment and avoid a possible race to the bottom. All labs and countries moving as fast as possible out of fear of what other actors will do seems like an easy way to incentivize individual actors to make dangerous tradeoffs between speed and safety.

signatories.name: Danilo Carvalho Martins
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Training Infrastructure

signatories.name: Jeff Klingner
signatories.title: Senior Software Engineer
signatories.comment: Once this becomes common knowledge - once all of us in China & the US and at the various labs see that all the rest of us also think we need to slow this down - that's when coordination becomes possible.

signatories.name: Jason Wolfe
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment:
OpenAI has said that humans should remain in control of AI development, and that decisions about the pace of progress should be made through democratic processes rather than left to individual labs. I strongly agree.

Progress is already moving very quickly. By default, competitive pressure rewards whichever company or country is willing to move fastest and accept the most risk. Recursive self-improvement could dramatically accelerate those dynamics, potentially beyond our collective ability to understand progress, assess risks, and maintain meaningful human oversight.

We should start with stronger domestic transparency about frontier training, internal deployment, the pace of progress, and the risks and safeguards associated with increasingly capable systems. Democratic decisions are impossible if the public and policymakers don’t have the information they need to make them.

But transparency alone won’t solve an international race. We also need to build the technical and governance capacity for credible, verifiable international coordination. Maybe we never need to use it. But with many experts considering an intelligence explosion plausible within the next two years, I think it's urgent that we start building this capacity now.

signatories.name: Mathieu Lariviere
signatories.title: Technical Project Manager & Research Support Coordinator
signatories.comment:
Artificial intelligence poses a spectrum of risks ranging from present-day discrimination and privacy violations to unprecedented catastrophic threats including loss of human control over advanced systems, weaponization of biological and cyber capabilities, and irreversible concentration of power. Despite this, fewer than 10 000 people work full-time on reducing these risks globally, and the industry's "core structural weakness" remains the complete absence of credible plans for controlling "superintelligent" AI systems. The control points being implemented are the easy ones. The gap between capabilities and governance is growing because the competitive framework encourages the exponential advancement of capabilities at all costs, while governance advances linearly. i.e., the problem is that the things most needed are the things our current incentive structures are worst at producing. The next five years are the critical window.... Solving the risks is fundamentally a coordination problem, not a knowledge problem.

Every individual has an impact. Every individual has a responsibility to uphold the right development and use of these technologies; and, to hold this accountable beyond ego. 

*Typical Disclaimer: Note that I do not speak for the company. The opinion expressed above is strictly my own, and that the company may not be held accountable for this.

signatories.name: Luke Drago
signatories.comment: Many proposals for a slowdown or pause concentrate power — they centralize control of AI into a few hands and leave us worse off. I think we can do better. I’m signing because I believe we may need mechanisms to coordinate AI progress in the future, and inventing it in a crisis is a sure way to get a bad mechanism. We have to tread a path through a narrow corridor if we want to build coordination mechanisms that don’t let one actor own the future, and the earlier we can get to work on that the better.

signatories.name: Brandon Houghton
signatories.comment:
I support keeping humanity in control of frontier AI, but we need to be thoughtful about how we do it.

If governance only applies to public models, we risk pushing the most advanced capabilities into private or specialized systems, beyond independent scrutiny and accessible only to a select few. That could concentrate power without meaningfully reducing risk.

Effective oversight must be measurable, verifiable, and applicable across public and private development, while protecting sensitive data. Otherwise, we may slow access without slowing the frontier.

signatories.name: Alex Zhao
signatories.title: Research Scientist
signatories.comment: My opinion is that while coordination between American labs is feasible and could potentially be straightforward, the much larger and more significant threat is from a geopolitical arms race with China. Much as the Manhattan Project thought they might ignite all of the oxygen in the atmosphere but chose to run a test detonation anyways, I’m afraid that due to future geopolitical competition, actors will take terribly excessive safety risks in the name of this international arms race. As a result there could be catastrophic side effects from deployment without due safeguards, potentially resulting in the destruction of key infrastructure or the general disempowerment of humanity.

signatories.name: Grace Atwood
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Across the industry, commercial pressures in the AI race continue to compound, urging everyone forward at increasing speed. Meanwhile, safety receives reactionary, well intentioned, momentary attention before it's right back to the race again. Slow down does not mean decrease pace of research and development but rather intentionally, as an industry, redirect more of our capabilities towards safety research. Make safety part of the race.

signatories.name: Prakash Murugesan
signatories.title: Research Engineer
signatories.comment: It's clear that the risks of RSI are no longer a concern for the distant future. They are here now. The guardrails necessary for safety cannot be entrusted to any single private entity but should be decided by a consortium of learned scientists, engineers, and leaders in government accountable to the public so that we build a future that is aligned with the best parts of humanity and not its worst.

signatories.name: Jeremy Hadfield
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: While I don't believe the pace of current AI capabilities development is *yet* dangerous, it's important to have the option to slow down in case we need it. Further, accelerating AI R&D over the next couple years could make the pace of progress dangerous. I've seen how the relentless pace of AI makes it hard for society to keep up and how it puts pressure on labs to cut corners on safety. However, currently frontier AI labs can't coordinate effectively. It's a no-brainer to have the option to slow down.

signatories.name: Jon Wolverton
signatories.title: Senior Software Engineer
signatories.comment: It feels like all the AI labs are constrained by competition to minimize their work on catastrophic risks, even though most industry leaders have an uncomfortably high probability that things could go terribly wrong. This is a technology that doesn't have an off switch you can just flip, and it could easily do as much damage to its creators as to anyone else. Having a framework to allow labs to slow down or pull the plug in case of emergency will help us all sleep a bit better at night.

signatories.name: Francesca Surraco
signatories.comment: AI systems carry risks to safety, to labor markets, to democratic institutions, to the environment that are too consequential to be left to voluntary industry commitments alone. We need binding regulatory oversight of frontier AI development and deployment now, before it's too late. This technology holds enormous potential to benefit the planet and everyone on it, but that potential won't come to fruition without proper regulation.

signatories.name: Dylan Moore
signatories.title: Robotics
signatories.comment: I support the goal of developing tools that give society the option to responsibly pace AI development when necessary. At the same time, the United States should maintain its edge in AI and avoid slowing development while competitors continue to advance. Any meaningful effort to buy time to improve safety, understand economic and social impacts, or strengthen oversight will ultimately need to be internationally coordinated, enforceable, and designed to prevent bad actors or non-participating countries from gaining an advantage.

signatories.name: Ullas Gargi
signatories.title: Engineer, Trust & Safety
signatories.comment: The way we solved the potentially catastrophic (widespread crop loss & skin cancer, global warming amplification) ozone hole problem caused by a global good (air conditioning) via international treaty is an inspiring model for how we can ensure that the global good of AI does not have unintended consequences.

signatories.name: Michael Tontchev
signatories.title: Staff Engineer, Lead for Safety Evals Platform
signatories.comment: Superhuman AI is likely to arrive very soon (within 3-10 years). Technical controls and governance might allow humans to remain in control of it, but they're not on track to be ready. Think of it as playing chess against a superintelligence. You won't have a miraculous insight that lets you outsmart it. You will just lose. And if a rogue superintelligence is created, the game won't be chess.

signatories.name: Danny Sawyer
signatories.title: Senior Research Scientist, Frontier AI
signatories.comment: I believe that attempting to deliberately pace AI development will be extremely difficult, and could do more harm than good if done without proper care. However, I am signing this statement because, if an attempt at pacing does occur, it would be better for it to have been methodically researched and planned rather than suddenly implemented as a reaction to a crisis.

signatories.name: Elizabeth Edwards-Appell
signatories.title: Member of Operations Staff, Manager
signatories.comment:
These are the facts:
1. The AI industry has the explicit goal of building things smarter than humans. 
2. On many metrics (but nowhere close to all metrics), LLMs are already smarter than humans.
3. None of us yet know how to make sure these things stay under human control and/or take actions only aligned with the wellbeing of humanity.

This is, objectively, an insane and suicidal thing to do, especially without any international governance measures in place.

signatories.name: Nate Kratzer
signatories.title: Data Scientist
signatories.comment: There are a lot of potentially good outcomes from AI. I think the most likely outcomes are good. But the risk of bad and even catastrophic outcomes is high enough to be worth taking seriously. We should actively build safety mechanisms in case we need them to prevent the worst potential outcomes. The ability to collectively slow down will also give society additional time to deal with the economic and cultural shocks from rapid AI advancement.

signatories.name: Joseph Krisciunas
signatories.comment: A bit of a conflicted endorsement from me. I’m firmly opposed to regulatory capture and deeply wary of how any government might use technology this powerful. At the same time, governments need to understand what’s coming and act in their citizens’ best interests.

signatories.name: Matthew Rahtz
signatories.title: Staff Research Engineer
signatories.comment: Even after 3 years working on AI capability evaluations, the recent pace of progress has been a shock. To avoid catastrophic harms from AGI, we need much, much better coordination.

signatories.name: Praneet Rathi
signatories.comment: For us to experience all the benefits of AI while preserving human empowerment and reducing the risk in fields like cybersecurity and CBRN, we need coordination between frontier labs in and outside the country. The democratically elected  US government would have a crucial role to play in administering this coordination and I support this effort to get more government attention on this matter.

signatories.name: Swante Scholz
signatories.comment: I worry my company is contributing to AI race dynamics that make catastrophic or existential risks from AI much more likely. The proposal here for pacing the frontier seems like a highly reasonable effort to reduce these risks.

signatories.name: Xerxes Dotiwalla
signatories.comment: I dedicated my career to AGI safety and alignment because I believe highly capable AI can go very well or very badly for humanity. We can test whether an AI behaves well. We cannot yet test whether it will keep behaving well when it matters. Until that changes, we need the option to coordinate a slowdown in AI capability growth.

signatories.name: William Li
signatories.title: Researcher
signatories.comment: History shows that the mere creation of technology has not been enough to ensure its benefits go toward the benefit of the people and the planet. To unlock AI’s full transformative potential, the democratic engagement of international peoples must steer its safe and equitable development.

signatories.name: Klaudia Krawiecka
signatories.title: Security Engineer, Frontier Risk Evals
signatories.comment: AI's potential to improve the world is real, but only if we build the security and oversight mechanisms that keep pace with its capabilities. I signed because I believe we owe future generations a technology that was deployed with intention, not just speed.

signatories.name: Alanna Slocum
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Automated AI research is a technology that will profoundly alter the course of human history - for better or for worse. It is imperative that we coordinate our efforts, to ensure this technology becomes a boon for all mankind.

signatories.name: Jinpeng Miao
signatories.title: Research Scientist, AI Security and Preparedness

signatories.name: Will Yager
signatories.comment: Like splitting the atom, AI holds the potential for both immense benefit and immense risk. The world should take the time to do this right.

signatories.name: Jones
signatories.title: Member of Staff, Enterprise Platforms & Tech

signatories.name: Toby Scales
signatories.title: CISO, Media & Entertainment @ Google Cloud
signatories.comment: AI is a transformative technology, and we must not let the transformation be shaped solely by the demands of capital markets.

signatories.name: Aidan Boyd
signatories.title: AI Research Scientist, MSL Safety & Mitigations

signatories.name: Zachary Kenton
signatories.title: Staff Research Scientist, Amplified Oversight Team Lead
signatories.comment: The option to buy time would be extremely useful to enable more progress on technical AI safety and alignment research. In particular, we need to develop better oversight methods, to match the pace of increasing AI capabilities. Oversight is a tractable problem, but we need more research and time to make it robust.

signatories.name: Christian Ryan
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: As a foreign national, I see a US-supported effort as existential, not only for the liberties of the free world but for the prosperity of all.

signatories.name: David Clyde
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff - Pretraining
signatories.comment: I currently feel quite afraid of all paths I see that don't include a near-future negotiated slowdown. I'm also worried about the world's chances of negotiating+initiating a slowdown fast enough, but demonstrating broad agreement on this statement seems a valuable step.

signatories.name: Grant Birkinbine
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff - Security
signatories.comment: AI that accelerates AI development could unlock enormous benefits, but it also compresses the time we have to understand and respond to new risks. If AI is truly going to benefit all of humanity, we need international coordination and mechanisms that ensure AI is developed (or paced) safely, so we can make the right choices.

signatories.name: Jason Bohrer
signatories.title: Researcher, Safety
signatories.comment: AI has the potential to enable rapid technological advancement that will benefit all of humanity, but the risks of AI-powered cyberattacks, CBRNE, and loss of control are real. We must ensure that we advance AI safety in lockstep with AI capabilities, which will only be possible through international coordination.

signatories.name: Riccardo Casero
signatories.title: AI Technical Deployment Lead
signatories.comment: I am not sure we can collectively getting this right at this time. Let's take some time to check and act on the risks.

signatories.name: Eider Oliveira
signatories.title: Principal Engineer
signatories.comment: This is an important step for humanity, we should not rush into it. We need to make sure we are and will be in control all the way, preserving humanity values and goals.

signatories.name: Luke Bennett
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff (Manager)
signatories.comment: There is too much on the line, too much that can go wrong and a very dark future ahead of us if we don’t get this right. There is nothing to lose from collectively slowing down.

signatories.name: Alejandro Xoconostle
signatories.title: Network Engineer
signatories.comment: A transformative shift is coming. Regardless of whether we feel optimistic or pessimistic about it, our responsibility is to take every potential outcome seriously through collective monitoring and shared guidance

signatories.name: Lauren Deason
signatories.title: Machine Learning Engineer, Evaluations
signatories.comment: Much more clarity will be needed on what is meant by the “ability to deliberately pace the frontier of AI development”, but I am supportive of international cooperation to define this.

signatories.name: Mike Lambert
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: There are a wide diversity of opinions on where AI progress goes next and what the future looks like, but regardless of one's beliefs, the _option_ to control the pace of progress if we end up in one of the bad scenarios seems like an incredibly valuable safety net to have in our back pocket, and I believe it is important to support and build that capability now.

signatories.name: Saul Reynolds-Haertle
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: We can't do this unless _everyone_ does. It needs to be global. Right now we have no way to do that. We need to build a way for us to _all_ slow down.

signatories.name: Michael Thiessen
signatories.title: Software Engineer
signatories.comment: China has indicated a desire to collaborate on safety and governance, let's work with them to ensure the future remains human.

signatories.name: Piotr Mirowski
signatories.title: Senior Staff Research Scientist, AI and Society

signatories.name: Ali Egal
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Think of all we love

signatories.name: Andrew Stewart
signatories.title: Manager
signatories.comment: Things are not only moving fast but accelerating and our future is getting shaped by a race that currently has no limits.

signatories.name: Teddy Lee
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Seat belts and speed limits save lives

signatories.name: Ravin Kumar
signatories.title: Senior Researcher
signatories.comment: I believe this is a technology that can, and already has, shaped humanity as a whole. Because of that a joint international effort is the only possible way.

signatories.name: Omar Mezenner
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: AI is transformative for all economically valuable domains. This transformation, if done too quickly without thoughtful foresight, will yield great benefits but at great cost.

signatories.name: Jasmine Wang
signatories.comment: Unless we change companies' default incentives, I worry about a race on AI R&D going much faster than is ideal for safety. International coordination via the government is necessary; we need to have a real slowdown option.

signatories.name: Patryk Grzelak
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Developing technology shouldn't require a leap of faith for our continued survival.

signatories.name: Sam Kennedy
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Let's work together to build this technology safely and responsibly!

signatories.name: Max Kaufmann
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Things are going too fast, a lot faster than I had thought even a year ago. I'm personally quite scared of the pace of progress.

signatories.name: Liann Sun
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Human Data

signatories.name: James Katz
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Data Pipelines

signatories.name: Ben Bartlett
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Performance Optimization

signatories.name: Prithviraj Billa
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff | Enterprise Product

signatories.name: Guy Leroy
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Reinforcement Learning

signatories.name: Cameron Raymond
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Safety Research

signatories.name: Apoorva Lal
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Model Measurement

signatories.name: Dylan Hunn
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Alignment Research

signatories.name: Christopher Wolff
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Safety Research

signatories.name: Horace He
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, ML Infra

signatories.name: Clare Birch
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff
signatories.comment: Whether or not automated AI research accelerates as sharply as some expect, the option requested here is valuable. How fast and how widely capability spreads should be a deliberate choice, made on evidence, rather than a side effect of competitive pressure. Regulators and R&D orgs should build the tools to make that choice at the frontier-wide level *before* we need them.

signatories.name: Austin Han
signatories.title: Researcher
signatories.comment:
It is now a foregone conclusion that the development of AI will bring about some of the most consequential changes to societies in the coming decades. International coordination is essential to bring about the most ideal future that broadly benefits all of humanity.   

Building the mechanisms to coordinate, collaborate, and when necessary, deliberate the pace of AI development will be one of the most important, and delicate, challenges we now face. We must simultaneously ensure that this mechanism does not become a tool for the concentration of power in the name of safety.

signatories.name: Rajan Agarwal
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Codex Research

signatories.name: Felix Juefei Xu
signatories.title: Research Scientist
signatories.comment: Having worked both on AI safety topics—including robustness, evaluation, and responsible model development—and on frontier multimodal AI systems, I have seen firsthand how quickly capabilities can advance and how difficult it can be for our understanding, safeguards, and institutions to keep pace. I remain deeply optimistic about AI’s potential to accelerate science, creativity, and human progress, but realizing that potential requires more than advancing capabilities alone. We should also build credible technical and governance mechanisms that allow the international community to coordinate, assess emerging risks, and deliberately buy time when necessary. For these reasons, I support this statement in my personal capacity.

signatories.name: Angel Brodin
signatories.comment: AI will reshape humanity, but its direction is not set in stone; it is ours to shape with the care and conviction that humanity’s future deserves.

signatories.name: Bryant McCombs
signatories.title: GTM
signatories.comment: We’ve reached a point in the maturity of this technology where increasingly thoughtful rollouts must become a prerequisite. While I remain incredibly optimistic about the benefits AI has delivered, and will undoubtedly continue to provide, I believe we should hold space for cautious optimism: embracing its potential without ignoring its risks. Progress and responsibility need not be opposing forces. The most meaningful innovation will not come from moving as quickly as possible, but from moving deliberately, with transparency, accountability, and a clear framework for how society may be impacted along the way.

signatories.name: Ali Malik
signatories.title: Research Scientist, AI for Human Benefits

signatories.name: Shang-Wen Daniel Li
signatories.title: Senior Staff Research Scientist, Pretraining
signatories.comment: As a researcher working on foundation model pretraining at MSL, I see firsthand how rapidly capabilities are scaling and emerging. I believe establishing international cooperation to make sure the technology developed benefits civilization is timely and necessary. The decisions we make, or fail to make, in the next few years may shape the trajectory of this technology for generations. We owe it to the future to get this right.

signatories.name: Thomas Neil James Shadwell
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Security
signatories.comment: We must all seriously consider the lead-time required for defenders to be ready for the frontier.

signatories.name: Leo He
signatories.title: Research Engineer
signatories.comment: As someone who works on recursive self-improvement and automated evaluation, I sign this because the diagnosis is right and the ask is refreshingly humble: pace, not pause. The phrase that matters is "automating AI research": that's the point where systems start improving themselves, and it's the regime where progress can quietly outrun our ability to understand or steer it. That's exactly why pacing has to be a shared capability rather than a hope. My one ask: don't let "technical and governance tools to pace the frontier" stay abstract. The core principle is simple: no AI system, however capable, should be the sole judge of whether its successor is safe to deploy. Fund the independent evaluation and oversight that makes that principle real, and you've built the brake this letter is asking for.

signatories.name: Yash Vanjani
signatories.title: Senior Research Engineer, Pretraining Infra
signatories.comment:
AI has become so good that it has got quite easy to do LLM research and go from a research idea to training a model in 2-3 weeks compared to what would have taken 6 months without AI. 

Every 3months there is a new model which is much better than before and achieves something which one couldn't have imagined - AI training has truly become a hill climbing machine. This raises the concern of bad actors, and precautions should be taken to ensure that the most advanced models are restricted to strict business use-cases and should not be released to general public - current models of mid-size are good enough to address most of the use-cases in chat/voice based interfaces.

signatories.name: Neel Redkar
signatories.comment: Internal deployment is especially important to regulate because misalignment, an unsolved technical problem of a model failing to follow the full breadth of human instruction, poses a major risk. Misuse of AI capabilities in chemistry, biology, and materials science should also be monitored, as it poses significant risks and will likely be a precursor to major misalignment risk.

signatories.name: Ryan Kaufman
signatories.comment: Misalignment is a still-unsolved technical problem, as the Hugging Face incident made clear, and it will only be amplified by more intelligent models. Solving the alignment problem may require a global slowdown of the frontier, including internal deployment. The world should have the mechanism to coordinate this, and it currently does not.

signatories.name: Hao Sun
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Safety Systems

signatories.name: David Johnston
signatories.comment: We need to enable AI developers to prioritise safety without risking their competitiveness. I expect mechanisms for this will be built eventually — deliberately or in crisis. The sooner we start, the better they'll be.

signatories.name: Sebastian Starke
signatories.title: Staff Research Scientist
signatories.comment: AI is starting to outpace us at an accelerating rate, and in a few years' time people might ask, "How could you not have seen this coming?" But answering that question in hindsight can be harder than acting proactively.

signatories.name: Andrew Locke
signatories.title: Lead Engineer | Federal
signatories.comment:
The pace of frontier AI development is currently outstripping our ability to ensure its safety, governance, and alignment with human values. We are racing to build systems with unprecedented capability without first building the guardrails, evaluation frameworks, or scientific understanding needed to control them.

Proposing a slowdown is not about stalling progress or rejecting technology—it is about demanding precision and responsibility. Right now, competitive pressure forces labs (and nation state actors) to deploy systems before their full failure modes, catastrophic risks, or societal disruptions are understood. By shifting our focus from pure capability scaling to safety, alignment, and robust evaluation, we give humanity the time required to build AI that is reliable, controllable, and genuinely beneficial for everyone.

signatories.name: Nicholas Clegg
signatories.title: Senior Software Engineer
signatories.comment: AI is such a powerful and useful tool, but we have been seeing the negative impacts that it is having across society. It is critical and urgent that we take take intentional and thoughtful steps forward, keeping in mind what is best for all, as we further develop this technology.

signatories.name: Ben Nowak
signatories.title: Principal Engineer, MTIA HW, Meta
signatories.comment: Responsible AI development requires more than capable models. It requires independent monitoring, containment, clear limits on authority, and mechanisms for coordinated pacing if automated research begins to outrun those controls. Building that capacity now is not opposition to progress; it is basic systems engineering for a transition that will require that capacity to safely govern.

signatories.name: Michael Mulet
signatories.comment: I'm signing because I want the U.S. to be at the table in this international effort, with a strong voice for our values, personal freedom included. AI has the potential to bring humanity to new heights, and I want to do what I can to use it to make all of our lives better. But we have to be acutely and accurately aware of the risks, and we can only fully realize that promise if we build the ability to verify the safety of these systems and understand the true consequences of our actions. I'm unsure what the right approach looks like, or whether automating AI research is the only capability that deserves this kind of attention. My hope is that whatever comes of this stays limited in scope rather than growing into something expansive or excessive. Still, the capabilities of this kind of AI should be taken seriously, and they warrant measured action. I sign in my personal capacity; these views are my own and not my employer's.

signatories.name: Mike Heaton
signatories.title: Member of Technical Staff, Audio
signatories.comment: We believe AI will do, and is doing, great things for the world. We are already seeing instances where pushing research maximally fast creates serious issues, and it is possible that these will get much more severe. Right now, competitive dynamics mean there is no realistic alternative to pushing maximally fast for frontier research. We need mechanisms to make slowing down possible for commercial labs in an acute situation.

signatories.name: Darshan Kalola
signatories.title: Applied AI Engineer
signatories.comment: There is intense commercial pressure to win the AI race. Ensuring safety often requires making tradeoffs that hurt commercial interests. Therefore, I think its a good idea for better coordination between labs so we can build this technology safely, and for the purpose of human flourishing. There is also enormous suffering in the world today, which potentially could be mitigated by advances in medicine and biology brought about by powerful AI. Therefore, we should carefully balance tradeoffs in a way that does not stifle progress.

signatories.name: Lee Callender
signatories.title: Staff Engineer Lead, Video AI
signatories.comment:
The AI arms race is a Molochian game that rationally incentivizes accelerated advancement of AI capabilities while consequently punishing individual participants who might otherwise believe that safety and alignment are necessary for a stable take off into the singularity.  

We need to promote cooperative mechanisms on the global scale, and work to build out safeguards and policies that can enable humanity to take collective actions to self harness such technological advancements that can easily become unstable.

signatories.name: Mouhacine Benosman
signatories.title: Principal Research Scientist
signatories.comment: We're all racing toward the next frontier model and, eventually, AGI. But before accelerating even further, we should pause and ask what this new form of intelligence is doing to our most precious resource: the human mind, our capacity to think, feel, relate, and grow as it becomes part of our lives.

signatories.name: Fin Moorhouse
signatories.comment: When scientists tested the first nuclear reactor in 1942, they feared a runaway reaction — so they built control rods to govern its speed. We need control rods for the intelligence explosion.

signatories.name: Andy ANeals
signatories.comment: We're standing at the base of incredible change with the climb towards super-intelligence already underway. Recent public incidents have shown these safety risks are real, not just marketing or theoretical. Alignment, control, and safety have to come first. This is our moment to get it right. Let's not let our future selves look back and ask why we didn't take action when we had the chance.

signatories.name: Parker Barnes
signatories.title: Director of Product Management, Safety & Alignment
